performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does a rondo of loud and quiet themes build a monument out of sound?
intro: A gate that was never built becomes the suite’s finale: a grand theme, a quiet chant, bells, the Promenade, and a long climax. Follow the alternation of loud and hushed. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: The gate theme returns
sections.mNote: the grand theme again, at full strength

sections.label: Quiet hymn again
sections.mNote: after a pause of nearly three seconds

sections.label: The gate theme in full
sections.mNote: grand theme enters after a short silence

sections.label: Closing climax
sections.mNote: the theme returns for the last, longest climax

cues.title: A proud brass opening
cues.text: A proud, brass-heavy opening leads to a majestic theme for the full orchestra, juxtaposed with softer woodwinds. It is the walking Promenade theme with its uneven bars evened out: the visitor has arrived at the gate.
cues.evidence: Proud brass-heavy opening, majestic orchestral theme and softer woodwinds: Philharmonia guide (Joanna Wyld). The Promenade’s metre evened out: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (movement 10). Relative level −10.7 to −12.7 dB over 0:00–0:25 with under one attack a second.

cues.title: A softer wind answer
cues.text: At about 0:30 the sound softens and thins: the level drops by some five decibels and the attacks all but stop. Softer woodwinds answer the brass before the full theme gathers again towards 0:45.
cues.evidence: Relative level −12.7 dB (0:25), −17.4 (0:30), −12.3 (0:35), −17.3 (0:40), then −8.3 dB at 0:45; onsets per second 0.0 at 0:30. Softer woodwinds answering the brass: Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: A gate that was never built
cues.text: Hartmann designed monumental gates for Kyiv, to commemorate Alexander II’s narrow escape from assassination on 4 April 1866. His design won the competition, but the gate was not built. Mussorgsky’s finale is a picture of it. See the Hartmann edge.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (movement 10): Hartmann’s design for Alexander II’s escape on 4 April 1866, winning the competition, cancellation; Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note: the gates were never built. Linked edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874. The note sits at the end of the first loud statement (−8.9 dB at 0:55).

cues.title: Dedicated to Stasov
cues.text: Five days after finishing the suite, Mussorgsky inscribed it to Vladimir Stasov, the critic who had helped organise the Hartmann memorial exhibition. A month later he added a note that he meant to publish it; it did not appear until Rimsky-Korsakov’s edition of 1886.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article, sections “Composition history” (dedication to Stasov five days after 22 June; publication intention a month later) and “Publication history” (1886, Rimsky-Korsakov). The note sits in the hushed hymn (−30 dB, 1:15–1:30).

cues.title: The theme comes back
cues.text: At about 1:37 the grand theme returns: the level jumps from −30 dB to −11 dB within two seconds. This second statement is the shape the opening promised, as a rondo; keep the hymn’s quiet in mind.
cues.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −29.7 dB at 1:36, −16.7 dB at 1:37 and −11.2 dB at 1:38, a rise of about 18 dB in two seconds; the 5-second table shows −30.7 dB (1:30) and −19.8 dB (1:35), −11.7 dB (1:40). Boundaries at 1:28 and 1:32 (novelty 0.91 each). The rondo shape ABAB–CADA: Wikipedia’s article.

cues.title: A pause before the hymn
cues.text: At about 2:11 the sound stops almost completely for nearly three seconds, the longest silence in the movement. The chant then returns, quiet, for its second appearance.
cues.evidence: A near-silence between 2:10.8 and 2:13.7, about 2.9 s, more than 30 dB below the loudest passage, in a frame-by-frame level pass; the 5-second table shows −9.7 dB at 2:00 and −32.4 dB at 2:10. The hymn’s second appearance follows the ABAB pattern (Wikipedia).

cues.title: Hartmann’s own favourite
cues.text: Hartmann thought the gate design the best work he had done. Steinberg describes tinted brick, an imperial eagle on top, and a three-storey belfry with a cupola shaped like a Slavonic helmet. The finale supplies its own bells.
cues.evidence: Hartmann’s opinion: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (movement 10). The brick, eagle, belfry and helmet-shaped cupola: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note; bells in the music: LA Phil note (Orrin Howard). The drawing: File:Hartmann -- Plan for a City Gate.jpg (content/art.json). The note sits in the second hymn (−38 to −30 dB, 2:11–2:44).

cues.title: A new idea with bells
cues.text: The pattern ABAB is broken by new music at about 2:46: the level steps up to about −23 dB and holds a steady sound with almost no new attacks, with E♭ and B recurring among the strongest pitches. LA Phil’s note hears “the clanging of bells”.
cues.evidence: Relative level −32.1 dB at 2:44 to −22.7 dB at 2:47, then steady near −20 dB to 3:05 with almost no attacks; boundary at 2:38 (novelty 0.64). E♭ and B are among the top three pitch classes in the 5-second table at 2:50, 2:55, 3:00 and 3:05. Bells: LA Phil note (Orrin Howard); the interruption of ABAB by new music: Wikipedia. The report does not identify bells.

cues.title: The Promenade returns
cues.text: Somewhere in the long build before the final theme, the Promenade is heard again; in Laki’s words it leads directly into the final climax. Listen through the steady rise from about −21 dB at 3:05 to −12 dB at 3:25.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note: near the end the Promenade theme is heard, leading directly into the final climax; LA Phil note: the Promenade theme among the movement’s ingredients. Relative level −21.7 dB (3:05), −17.7 (3:10), −15.0 (3:15), −12.3 (3:25). The report does not identify the theme or its time, so the cue places no event at a moment.

cues.title: A gap, then the grand theme
cues.text: At about 3:51 there is a brief silence, less than a second long. Then the grand theme arrives in full, near −7 dB by 3:53, at the start of its last great run.
cues.evidence: A near-silence between 3:51.4 and 3:52.1 in a frame-by-frame level pass; a 1-second pass gives −13.7 dB at 3:50, −36.0 dB at 3:51, −13.5 dB at 3:52 and −6.8 dB at 3:53. The grand theme’s return after a shimmering march: Philharmonia guide. The gate theme’s final appearances follow ABAB–CADA (Wikipedia).

cues.title: A hush, then the longest climax
cues.text: At about 4:19 the level drops sharply from −14 dB to −24 dB; from 4:26 it climbs again through −20, −16 and −10 dB to −5.5 dB at 4:42. This is the build to the last statement, at the peak of the finale.
cues.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −14.0 dB at 4:18, −24.5 dB at 4:19, −24.2 dB at 4:25, −17.5 dB at 4:27, −9.6 dB at 4:40 and −5.5 dB at 4:42; boundaries at 4:22, 4:34 and 4:44 (novelty 0.36, 0.39, 0.48). The shimmering march that unveils the main theme before the triumphant ending: Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: Ravel brings it to Paris
cues.text: Ravel made his orchestration in 1922 for Serge Koussevitzky, whose commission gave him sole conducting rights for several years. Koussevitzky first recorded it in 1930 with the Boston Symphony and made it a repertory piece.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (arrangements: Koussevitzky commission, sole conducting rights for several years, first recording in 1930 with the Boston Symphony Orchestra); Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note on the 1922 commission and the 1930 recording. Linked edge: mussorgsky--ravel-pictures-orchestration. The note sits in the final build (−17 to −9 dB, 4:27–4:40).

cues.title: The last statements
cues.text: In the last twenty-five seconds the level stays high between about −9 and −6 dB, with one dip at 5:20 before it surges again. The orchestra ends at full strength at about 5:26.
cues.evidence: Relative level −8.7 to −10.7 dB across 5:10–5:20 in the 5-second table, then a 1-second pass: −9.6 dB (5:19), −17.4 (5:20), −9.4 (5:22), −5.9 (5:26) and −11.4 dB at 5:27. The report does not identify chords; “triumphant ending”: Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Brass fall silent; a chant begins
transitions.how: The first statement ends and, within a second, the level falls by about eighteen decibels. The brass-led grandeur gives way to a quiet, chorale-like theme in softer woodwinds, based on a Russian Orthodox baptismal chant. The join is the movement’s main device: loud and quiet statements alternate, like the façade of the gate and a chapel inside it.
transitions.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −11.9 dB (1:00), −30.4 dB (1:01), −32.7 dB (1:02); strongest boundary 1:02 (novelty 1.00); brightness 1,003 Hz to 561 Hz. The baptismal hymn: Wikipedia’s article; softer woodwinds: Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: The hymn is answered by the whole orchestra
transitions.how: After thirty seconds of quiet, almost without new attacks, the level jumps from about −30 dB to −11 dB within two seconds and the grand theme returns at full strength. Mussorgsky repeats the loud-quiet pairing, so the listener hears the gate theme as a return, not an arrival.
transitions.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −29.7 dB (1:36), −16.7 dB (1:37), −11.2 dB (1:38), a rise of about 18 dB in two seconds; boundaries at 1:28 and 1:32 (novelty 0.91 each). The recurrence follows the rondo shape (Wikipedia); the report cannot confirm the melody.

transitions.title: A silence of nearly three seconds
transitions.how: After the second grand statement the music stops almost completely for nearly three seconds, near 2:11. The quiet hymn then returns. The orchestra is not fading: the loud theme is cut off at about −10 dB and replaced by silence, which is a general pause. The pause makes the hushed chant sound like something heard after the crowd has gone.
transitions.evidence: A near-silence between 2:10.8 and 2:13.7 (about 2.9 s) in a frame-by-frame level pass; a 1-second pass gives −10.5 dB at 2:09, −20.0 at 2:10 and −38.1 at 2:11. Boundary at 2:14 (novelty 0.83). The hymn’s return: the ABAB pattern in Wikipedia’s article.

transitions.title: New music breaks the pattern
transitions.how: The pattern of loud theme and quiet hymn, set up twice, is interrupted. The level steps up to a steady −22 dB with almost no new attacks, and E♭ and B recur among the strongest pitches, a bell-like sound that LA Phil’s note calls “the clanging of bells”. Without a driving rhythm the movement gains space instead of progress. This C section extends the finale into a vast closing arch.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 2:38 (novelty 0.64); relative level −32.1 dB (2:44) to −22.7 dB (2:47), then steady near −20 dB to 3:05; E♭ and B among the top three pitch classes at 2:50–3:05. “Clanging of bells”: LA Phil note. The ABAB–CADA shape: Wikipedia’s article; no bell is timed by the report.

transitions.title: A pause, then the theme in full
transitions.how: The long build holds at about −13 dB, then the sound falls to near silence for under a second at about 3:51. The grand theme enters at full strength, and the level jumps by about seven decibels within a second. This is a short general pause followed by an arrival: the gate theme finally sounds with all the weight that has been gathered.
transitions.evidence: A near-silence between 3:51.4 and 3:52.1 in a frame-by-frame level pass; a 1-second pass gives −13.7 dB (3:50), −36.0 (3:51), −13.5 (3:52), −6.8 (3:53); the 5-second table shows −16.2 dB at 3:50 and −9.1 dB at 3:55. Philharmonia guide: the main theme returns after a shimmering march. No bar alignment is claimed.

transitions.title: Hush, then the last and longest build
transitions.how: The grand theme ends at about 4:18 and the level falls from −14 dB to −24 dB within two seconds. A hushed interlude follows, then the final build: the level climbs through −17 dB, −10 dB and −5.5 dB by 4:42. It is the movement’s last contrast of quiet and loud, and its peak ends the suite at full strength.
transitions.evidence: A 1-second pass gives −14.0 dB (4:18), −24.5 dB (4:19), −24.2 (4:25), −17.5 (4:27), −9.6 (4:40), −5.5 (4:42); boundaries at 4:22, 4:34 and 4:44 (novelty 0.36, 0.39, 0.48). The Philharmonia guide describes the building to a triumphant ending; the report cannot identify the music.

fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (5:29; this file is 5:28), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
